name: Representation Technique / Dissection (Howgrave-Graham-Joux, Becker-Coron-Joux)
description: The representation technique for hard (density ~1) knapsacks, introduced by Howgrave-Graham and Joux (EUROCRYPT 2010) and refined by Becker-Coron-Joux (EUROCRYPT 2011) and Bonnetain-Bricout-Schrottenloher-Shen (ASIACRYPT 2020). Instead of a two-way MITM split, the solution vector is represented in many different ways (e.g., as a signed/4-valued combination of partial vectors, allowing overlaps and the value 2), which 'bloats' the search space but multiplies the number of encodings of each true solution even more. By counting representations and filtering pseudo-solutions with modular/parity constraints, the enumeration per side is reduced. For random knapsacks of density close to 1 this gives heuristic running times O*(2^(0.337n)) (HGJ, 2010; long-version analysis 2^(0.3113n)), O*(2^(0.291n)) (BCJ, 2011), and O*(2^(0.283n)) (Bonnetain et al., 2020). The method is average-case/heuristic: the representation-counting argument needs random-like instances and is not a worst-case algorithm.
worst_case_time: No worst-case bound: the representation method is heuristic/average-case. Its running times are stated for random hard knapsacks of density ~1: O*(2^(0.337n)) (HGJ 2010; the ePrint long version 2010/189 states 2^(0.3113n) for almost all density-1 knapsacks), improved to O*(2^(0.291n)) (BCJ 2011) and O*(2^(0.283n)) (Bonnetain et al. 2020). For arbitrary worst-case instances no O*(2^((1/2-eps)n)) guarantee follows.
space_complexity: HGJ: O*(2^(0.256n)) memory (per BCJ's citation). BCJ retain low memory and additionally give a constant-memory variant based on cycle finding running in O(2^(0.72n)) time, plus an explicit time-memory tradeoff. Bonnetain et al. also discuss memory reductions. Schroeppel-Shamir-style O*(2^(n/4)) space is the prior baseline for the density-1 setting.
model: Classical RAM / word RAM (heuristic, with modular arithmetic). The same representation framework has been adapted to quantum walk algorithms (Bernstein-Jeffery-Lange-Meurer), but the HGJ/BCJ algorithms themselves are classical.
randomized_or_deterministic: Randomized, and heuristic/Monte Carlo: the complexity estimates assume random instances of density ~1 and the analysis is not fully rigorous for arbitrary inputs. There is no proven worst-case success guarantee; the algorithms are expected to succeed with high probability on random instances.
time_space_tradeoff_curve: BCJ present a time-memory tradeoff and a constant-memory variant (cycle finding) at O(2^(0.72n)) time; the main point is O~(2^(0.291n)) time with O~(2^(0.256n)) memory. Dissection (a closely related family, Dinur et al.) provides explicit worst-case time-space tradeoffs, unlike the basic representation method.
numerical_exponent_and_record_year: 0.337n (Howgrave-Graham-Joux, 2010, EUROCRYPT; the ePrint long version gives 0.3113n); 0.291n (Becker-Coron-Joux, 2011, EUROCRYPT); 0.283n (Bonnetain-Bricout-Schrottenloher-Shen, 2020, ASIACRYPT, using representations with values in {-1,0,1,2}).
problem_variant: Hard knapsack / random Subset Sum with density close to 1 (the cryptanalytic regime). Not the general worst-case vanilla Subset Sum, and not a promised-solution pigeonhole variant, though solutions exist with constant probability for density-1 instances.
applies_to: Random (or 'almost all') density-~1 knapsacks, i.e., cryptographic hard-knapsack instances; also generalized subset-sum/balancing settings after adaptation. Requires overlap-friendly representations, so it does not directly cover worst-case {0,1} Subset Sum.
coefficient_set: The original Subset Sum has C = {0,1}. The representation scheme represents each solution with coefficient vectors over larger signed sets: HGJ/BCJ use overlaps with values in {-1,0,1} (and related); Bonnetain et al. use {-1,0,1,2}. The effective 'coefficient set' is a design parameter of the representation, not the input domain.
density_regime: Density d = n / log2(max |a_i|) close to 1 (the hard-knapsack regime), where lattice-based low-density attacks fail. The method is designed for this density; low-density instances are easy by lattice reduction.
solution_regime: Assumes solutions (or many solutions) with overwhelming probability, as holds for random density-1 instances; it is a hard-instance/random-instance algorithm rather than a general decision procedure.
cardinality_constraint: Yes, in effect: balanced (fixed Hamming-layer) solutions are central. Representations are built around a chosen weight (e.g., splitting a weight-n/2 solution into weight-n/4 halves), and the representation count is a binomial coefficient such as C(n/2, n/4) ~ 2^(n/2)/sqrt(n). Cardinality/weight constraints are the main lever.
key_technique: Representation bloat plus filtering: (1) choose a representation format (overlaps, signed coefficients, and value 2) so a single solution has many encodings; (2) count the expected number of representations to choose parameters; (3) impose modular/parity filters that eliminate 'pseudo-solutions' (candidate pairs that satisfy the sum condition but combine to an invalid coefficient vector); (4) search the reduced, filtered lists. Related dissection recursively splits the problem into constrained subproblems; Nederlof-Wegrzycki and Chen-Jin-Randolph-Servedio adapted these ideas to worst-case and to Orthogonal Vectors.
core_idea: MITM matches two 2^(n/2) lists. If instead one deliberately enlarges the candidate space (e.g., allowing overlaps or signed coefficients), a genuine solution acquires exponentially many representations, more than the extra candidates added. Filtering then leaves only a small fraction to compare, so the per-side enumeration can be below 2^(n/2). BCJ further use pseudo-solutions to prune, and 4-valued representations (Bonnetain et al.) lower the exponent to 0.283. The intuition is that structure (many representations of one solution) beats the brute-force 2^(n/2) wall on random instances.
reduction_pipeline: Reduce Subset Sum to finding many collision/representation pairs, typically after a modular filter (mod 2^k) or low-weight representation constraint; equivalent to a generalized-birthday/collision problem and related to Wagner's algorithm. Dissection recursively generates lists; the worst-case adaptations reduce to Orthogonal Vectors (Nederlof-Wegrzycki) and to pseudo-solution recovery (Randolph-Wegrzycki).
constructive_vs_existential: Constructive (returns a witness vector when the heuristic succeeds), but the guarantee is only heuristic/average-case; constructivity is not proved for arbitrary worst-case inputs.
search_vs_decision_witness: Search/witness: returns the knapsack solution vector. Correctness/constructivity holds with high probability on random density-1 instances; no worst-case witness guarantee.
obstacle_to_2n3: The technique relies essentially on average-case structure: the representation-counting step needs each solution to have enough encodings, which random density-1 instances provide but structured/worst-case instances (notably {0,1} Subset Sum, Partition, C={-1,1}) may not. So it yields no worst-case O*(2^((1/2-eps)n)) bound, let alone 2^(n/3). Moreover its exponents (0.337 -> 0.291 -> 0.283) are still far above 1/3 and the analyses are heuristic. Reaching 2^(n/3) would need a rigorous worst-case representation theory (mixing, flexible representations, pseudo-solution recovery) and a way to guarantee representations for adversarial inputs; Randolph-Wegrzycki (STOC 2026) achieve worst-case mixing for many coefficient sets but explicitly cannot break the MITM barrier for C={-2,-1,1,2} and C={-1,1} (Partition).
potential_to_break_mitm: Low for worst-case Subset Sum (the method is inherently average-case); high for cryptanalytic average-case knapsacks (where it is state of the art). The worst-case transfer is a separate, harder line (mixing/flexible representations) and remains blocked for {0,1} Subset Sum and Partition.
barrier_evidence: The representation method's analysis is heuristic and explicitly average-case; no worst-case improvement follows. Worst-case representation arguments require the solution to have many encodings, which adversarially structured instances can deny. The k-SUM/3SUM/4SUM conjectures and SETH-based pseudo-polynomial lower bounds bound what structure exploitation can do; ETH only rules out 2^(o(n)). Randolph-Wegrzycki show the representation technique can be made worst-case for many constant coefficient sets but not for C={-1,1} (Partition) or C={-2,-1,1,2}; Equal Subset Sum needed separate progress. This is direct evidence that the average-case technique does not automatically carry over.
open_questions: Can representation methods be made fully worst-case for {0,1} Subset Sum? Is there a rigorous (non-heuristic) average-case analysis for HGJ/BCJ? Can the exponent be pushed below 2^(0.283n), and can any representation-based method reach 2^(n/3)? How should mixing and flexible representations be defined to survive adversarial inputs? Does a worst-case 2^((1/2-eps)n) algorithm for Partition/C={-1,1} exist?
conditional_hypothesis: The HGJ/BCJ complexity claims rest on heuristic randomness assumptions about density-1 instances (not a named hardness conjecture). Broader limits are governed by ETH (no 2^(o(n))), SETH-based pseudo-polynomial lower bounds (Abboud-Bringmann et al.), and the k-SUM/3SUM/4SUM conjectures. The average-case success probability is assumed, not proven, for arbitrary density-1 inputs.
worst_case_vs_average_case_guarantee: Average-case only (random / almost all density-1 knapsacks). Explicitly not a worst-case algorithm; the representation count can fail on structured instances. Worst-case versions exist only for related coefficient sets (Randolph-Wegrzycki) and not for {0,1} Subset Sum or Partition.
cryptographic_regime: Directly cryptographic: targets hard knapsacks of density ~1 with n generators, where lattice reduction (LLL/BKZ, Lagarias-Odlyzko) does not apply. Relevant to breaking knapsack-based cryptosystems and to the broader low-weight/decoding cryptanalytic frontier; the representation method is a standard cost model for such attacks.
pseudopolynomial_interaction: Complementary: the representation method is not pseudo-polynomial and is used for dense/high-density hard instances where DP is infeasible. It interacts with dense-subset-sum work (Austrin-Kaski-Koivisto-Nederlof, 'Dense Subset Sum may be the hardest') and with modular filters; proximity/Steinitz-style arguments appear in the worst-case transfer (Randolph-Wegrzycki).
key_references: N. Howgrave-Graham and A. Joux. New Generic Algorithms for Hard Knapsacks. EUROCRYPT 2010. ePrint 2010/189; https://eprint.iacr.org/2010/189 (abstract states 2^(0.3113n) for almost all density-1 knapsacks; the widely cited EUROCRYPT figure is 2^(0.337n) time / 2^(0.256n) memory)

A. Becker, J.-S. Coron, and A. Joux. Improved Generic Algorithms for Hard Knapsacks. EUROCRYPT 2011 (LNCS 6632:364-385). ePrint 2011/474; https://eprint.iacr.org/2011/474 (time O(2^(0.291n)); constant-memory variant O(2^(0.72n)))

X. Bonnetain, R. Bricout, A. Schrottenloher, and Y. Shen. Improved Classical and Quantum Algorithms for Subset-Sum. ASIACRYPT 2020 (LNCS 12492:633-666). ePrint 2020/168; https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/168 (O(2^(0.283n)) using representations with values in {-1,0,1,2})
P. Austrin, P. Kaski, M. Koivisto, and J. Nederlof. Dense Subset Sum may be the hardest. STACS 2016, 13:1-13:14. arXiv:1508.06019; https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.06019

T. Randolph and K. Wegrzycki. Beating Meet-in-the-Middle for Subset Balancing Problems. STOC 2026. arXiv:2511.10823; https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10823 (brings representation technique to worst case for many coefficient sets; leaves C={-2,-1,1,2} and C={-1,1}/Partition open)
X. Chen, Y. Jin, T. Randolph, and R. A. Servedio. Subset Sum in Time 2^(n/2)/poly(n). APPROX/RANDOM 2023. arXiv:2301.07134; https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.07134
empirical_evidence: HGJ and BCJ both report implementations demonstrating practicality on hard knapsacks; BCJ's abstract states 'An implementation shows the practicability of the technique.' Specific benchmark tables are not available in the abstracts and would require the full papers. [uncertain]
implementation_artifact: No clearly canonical public repository from the authors was located; the papers describe implementations but ready-to-run code is not obviously distributed (a Crypto StackExchange question explicitly asks for code implementing HGJ/BCJ attacks). Some independent implementations may exist. [uncertain]
verification_method: Reproduce the representation-counting argument (choose a representation format, count expected encodings and pseudo-solutions, derive the exponent) from the HGJ/BCJ full versions, then run the authors' algorithm on random density-1 knapsacks of increasing n and compare against Schroeppel-Shamir/MITM and brute force; also verify the claimed 2^(0.291n)/2^(0.283n) curves empirically. The worst-case claims of Randolph-Wegrzycki can be checked by following their mixing/flexible-representation proofs for the covered coefficient sets.
